Consider the safest therapies first: acetaminophen, mindfulness based therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, and exercise. B
Effective options for second-line therapy include anti-inflammatories, anti-depressants and anti-epileptic drugs. B
Third-line options include long-term opiates and surgical interventions such as sympathectomy for carefully selected and monitored patients. B

background.definition: Pain that persists beyond the usual time for an acute disease or a reasonable time for an injury to heal that is associated with chronic, pathologic processes that cause continuous pain or pain at intermittent intervals for months to years.

list.listitem: The National Center for Health Statistics estimates that 32.8% of the US general population has persistent or chronic pain.

There is no test to measure pain. Imaging correlates poorly with symptoms. The patient’s report of pain is your guide. C
Take a careful history of the pain and any preceding events.
Perform a thorough physical exam with attention to areas of pain.
Evaluate the patient’s functional status.
Evaluate the patient’s emotional response to pain.
Evaluate the patient for comorbid psychiatric disorders, including depression, anxiety disorder, and personality disorders.
Patients with impaired cognitive function pre-operatively are at greater risk of chronic pain post-operatively.
A has been validated for diagnosis of fibromyalgia.
Exercise is helpful for fibromyalgia and low back pain. B
There is evidence to support the effectiveness of mindfulness based therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy.B
Drug therapy for all types of pain starts with acetaminophen. For musculoskeletal or joint pain, NSAIDS can be tried if no contraindications. A
For neuropathic pain or fibromyalgia, tricyclic antidepressants or venlafaxine are preferred, followed by antiepileptics, such as carbamazepine. A
For pain that is uncontrolled, tramadol can be tried, followed by either short- or long-acting opioids. B

The Veteran's Administration and Department of Defense in the US have published evidence-based guidelines for appropriate use of opioids when managing patients with chronic pain. They include several one page algorithms to implement their recommendations.

Acetaminophen in full dose is the drug of choice because of its safety profile, although a recent systematic review found little or no evidence of benefit in patients with chronic low back pain. Similarly, a network meta-analysis also found no benefit of acetaminophen in patients with chronic knee and hip osteoarthritis. Acetaminophen should be avoided in patients with liver disease and used with caution in those who drink alcohol.

NSAIDs can be effective for musculoskeletal and joint pain, and a network meta-analysis concluded that diclofenac 150 mg/day was most likely to be effecitve for knee and hip osteoarthritis. NSAIDs should not be used in patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease, any GI bleeding, renal insufficiency, or those on anticoagulants. They should be used with caution in patients over 65 and those with cardiovascular disease. A study of 184 patients found similar efficacy between total daily doses of 1200 mg ibuprofen, 2400 mg ibuprofen, and 4000 mg acetaminophen in patients with chronic knee osteoarthritis.

A Cochrane review concluded that current evidence does not support the use of topical salicylate containing rubefacients. There have been several small trials showing that they were well tolerated with possible benefit, but they were at high risk of bias.

Tricyclic antidepressants and venlafaxine have been shown to be effective in neuropathic pain and are often the first choice in treating these conditions, with an NNT of approximately 3 and NNH between 16 and 28 for withdrawal from the study due to adverse effects. Duloxetine has also been approved for use in fibromyalgia and is effective for other neuropathic pain in doses of 60 to 120 mg daily, based on 18 clinical trials with 6407 patients (NNT = 5-8).

There is no clear evidences that antidepressants are effective in the treatment of chronic low back pain. A systematic review found evidence to support antidepressants for chronic rheumatic disorders.

A Cochrane review found 11 studies with 770 participants looking at anti-psychotics for acute and chronic pain in adults. They found a clinically meaningful benefit in terms of pain intensity compared with placebo (NNT = 3) but there was significant heterogeneity. The side effects of this drug class make it only appropriate for carefully selected patients and not as a first or even second line agent.

Carbamazepine, gabapentin, lamotrigine, and pregabalin are all used for chronic neuropathic pain and for fibromyalgia. However, a systematic review of 12 studies with 1511 participants concluded that lamotrigine is not effective for chronic neuropathic pain or fibromyalgia. While gabapentin is increasingly being used, the evidence suggests it is no more effective than carbamazepine.

A Cochrane review found three small studies of valproate or valproic acid for chronic pain, which were limited by reporting only of per protocol analysis (those who dropped out, perhaps due to adverse effects, were omitted). They found some evidence of efficacy but also adverse effects such as nausea, drowsiness, and elevated hepatic transaminases.
A randomized trial found no benefit to gabapentin in patients post knee arthroplasty.

A UK study identified 306 women age 18 to 50 years with chronic pelvic pain and randomized them to gabapentin or placebo. After 4 months, pain improved similarly in both groups, although those given gabapentin had significantly more dizziness and drowiness.

A large registry study found that gabapentin, when combined with high-dose opioid treatment, was associated with an increased risk of death among its users (2-3 additional deaths per 1000 person-years). The US FDA and the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency already require a warning about respiratory difficulties associated with gabapentin in patients with respiratory risk factors; adding it to another respiratory depressant, in this case opioid treatment, seems to increase rather than decrease the risk.

An umbrella Cochrane review found moderate to good quality evidence that duloxetine, milnacipran, and pregabalin were each effective in meaningful pain relief at 4 to 12 weeks. Long-term effectiveness data are lacking.

A systematic review identifed 30 RCTs (n = 1314) and 14 cohort studies (n = 1168) of skeletal muscle relaxants (SMRs) for patients with chronic pain. The most common SMRs were baclofen, tizanidine, and cyclobenzaprine. SMRs were no more effective than placebo for low back pain, fibromyalgia, and headaches. There was an association of significant improvement from SMRs for nocturnal leg cramps, trigeminal neuralgia, and chronic cervical pain. Common side effects that affected overall quality of life included drowsiness and dizziness.
Prednisolone is effective for complex regional pain syndrome, at least in the short term.

An ACP guideline (2025) concluded that the evidence is sparse regarding the use of cannabis or cannabinoids for chronic noncancer pain and this “advice” (which is different from a more rigid guideline) attempts, in a conservative way, to fill in the gaps. The authors suggest cautioning patients who are at risk of harm — young people, old people, pregnant people, and those with a current or past substance use disorder — to avoid these products. Let other patients know that the current evidence suggests only a small likelihood of benefit.

A systematic review found six small studies with a total of 226 adults comparing marijuana to control. Three of six studies reported clinically important improvements in pain, accompanied by significant neurocognitive side effects (i.e., getting high).
A comprehensive systematic review of medical cannabinoids concluded that there was moderate to high certainty supporting nabiximols for chronic pain.

A more recent systematic review identified 18 controlled trials with 1740 patients with chronic pain. They conclude that synthetic products containing THC, such as dronabinol or nabilone, or mixed THC and CBD products are associated with pain relief, and also sedation and dizziness, in patients with chronic neuropathic pain. The included studies were mostly of short duration.
A systematic review of 8 RCTs concluded that cannabinoids were effective with regards to sleep quality and pain intensity in patients with chronic neuropathic pain.
Opioids are considered 3rd line treatment for carefully selected and monitored patients.

American Academy of Neurology guidelines recommend tracking pain and function at every visit; documenting total daily morphine equivalent dose; screening for past and current depression, PTSD, anxiety, and substance abuse before prescribing; using random urine drug screening prior to initiation and during monitoring to assess for diversion; and avoiding escalation of doses above 80 to 120 mg/day.

CDC guidelines (2022) specifically state: "Recommendations are voluntary and are intended to support, not supplant, individualized, person-centered care. Flexibility to meet the care needs and the clinical circumstances of a specific patient is paramount." Further, they note that these recommendations are not intended to inform legislation or curtail clinical options for physicians. They note that opioids are not first-line for chronic pain and that other modalities should be used preferentially. They recommend immediate release over extended release opioids, at a starting dose of 5-10 morphine milligram equivalents (MME) per dose or 20-30 MME/day. One MME = 1 mg hydrocodone, 1.5 mg oxycodone, or 5 mg hydromorphone (so 10 mg oxycodone = 15 MME). As with the 2016 guidelines, advancing to more than 50 MME per day should be done cautiously and with careful patient education around harms and the danger of addiction.

Canadian guidelines recommend use of an Opioid Risk Tool to identify persons at increased risk of dependence, abuse, or diversion. The 2016 CDC guidelines recommend that (1) clinicians carefully weight benfits and harms, (2) that they focus on function rather than pain reduction, (3) that the lowest effective dose should be used, (4) that multidisciplinary teams and non-drug therapies be utilized, and (5) specialist consultation when daily doses exceed 50 to 90 morphine milligram equivalents.

ACP guidelines (2017) recommend NSAIDs as a first line medical therapy for chronic low back pain in non-medical therapies are ineffective, followed by tramadol or duloxetine. Opioids should only be considered after a careful discussion of potential benefits and harms, and only if all other treatments have failed.

Studies demonstrate significant efficacy of opioids over placebo. There is evidence suggesting that long-term treatment with opiates can lead to significant improvement in functional outcomes, including quality of life in patients with chronic, non-malignant pain. Concerns about overuse and diversion can be addressed with careful monitoring and the use of a controlled substances contract.

Tramadol is a weak opioid. A systematic review found 21 studies (N = 3205) compared tramadol with opioids, and 15 studies (N = 3931) compared tramadol with an NSAID. There were no significant differences between tramadol and opioids for efficacy, adverse events, or withdrawal due to adverse events. Compared with NSAIDs, tramadol was significantly more likely to result in withdrawals due to adverse events (RR 2.86), total withdrawals (RR 1.68), and total adverse events (RR 1.37). Tramadol was also less likely to provide a 30% or more reduction in pain from baseline (RR 0.82; 0.76 - 0.90).

Extended release morphine, extended release oxycodone, and transdermal fentanyl may be preferable to the short-acting opioids due to their longer duration of action, resulting in ease of use, fewer periods of uncontrolled pain, and less dose escalation. Diversion is a concern though, and many patients discontinue them due to adverse events or lack of efficacy. Cochrane review concluded that oral morphine is effective for cancer pain. Two Cochrane reviews found evidence for long-term opiates in patients with neuropathic (NNT = 4-6) or chronic non-malignant pain, accompanied by significant harms. Opiate switching strategies were poorly studied.

Hospitalizations and deaths have increased with increasing use of oxycodone and methadone for chronic non-malignant pain. The morphine equivalent dose has increased substantially, for example from 80 to 140 mg/day among injured workers from 1996 to 2002. Long-acting opioids were also associated with an increased risk of death due to causes other than overdose when used for non-cancer pain (167.1 vs 107.9 per 100,000 person-years) in an observational study using Tennessee Medicaid data.

A systematic review identified 28 studies with over 23 million patients looking at predictors of opioid overdose. Associations were found for having 3 or more prescribers (OR 4.7), a higher opioid dose (OR 2.6), a history of previous overdose (OR 5.9), using 4 or more pharmacies (OR 4.9), prescription of fentanyl (OR 2.8), and comorbid mental health disorders (OR 2.1 to 2.6).
A structured methadone program can be used for the treatment of chronic pain patients with opioids dependency, but side effects and serious adverse events may limit the beneficial effects.

Verbal clues during physician visits may indicate an openness to stopping or reducing opioid use. Clues were sorted into 5 categories: (1) pain: "[It] helps a little bit with the pain"; (2) function: "If I take two, I can't function"; (3) safety: "If I have to take more I'll be in serious trouble"; (4) side effects: "I don't like it"; and (5) personal identity: "I'm in a constant war with myself when I take pain medication."

A systematic review identified mostly low quality studies but identified prescriber interventions and pain self-management program as being potentially effective at reducing opioid dose in those using them chronically.

A trial randomized 193 opioid naiive adults following ACL reconstruction to 15, 25 or 35 oxycodone tablets. The researchers found no difference in pain (at rest, with activity, and overall pain), function, and satisfaction among the groups. There was also no difference in the morphine milligram equivalents consumed. Most patients from each of the 3 groups reported being “satisfied,” “very satisfied,” or “extremely satisfied” with the number of pills they received and 83% of patients who received 15 pills felt that they received the “right amount” or “too many."
Despite being effective for the treatment of opioid use disorder, buprenorphine was prescribed infrequently in the US. Patients receiving it were more likely to be male, white, and younger.

A study randomized 207 participants with chronic moderate to severe pain taking an average morphine equivalent daily dose of 150 mg to offer to switch to buprenorphine or continuing current treatment. Only 26% opted to switch, and a third of those switched back. If they did switch their opioid dose was significantly reduced.
A systematic review concluded that physician drug monitoring programs appear to decrease adverse opioid events.
Concurrent use of gabapentin with an opioid is associated with increased mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 2.03, 95% CI 1.2 to 3.5).
Botulinum toxin
A small randomized trial found no evidence to support the usef of botulinum toxin A injections for patients with chronic pelvic pain.
Surgical or chemical sympathectomy is based on very little high quality evidence. Complications may be significant, and more clinical trials are needed.

There is only limited evidence for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) as a treatment for chronic pain. A single small study found benefit for patients with bone pain who have cancer. Studies of TENS for osteoarthritis of the knee were inconclusive.
There is some evidence to support transcranial non-invasive brain stimulation techniques.

Spinal cord stimulation for chronic pain of neuropathic origin is recommended by NICE guidelines when patients have at least 6 months of moderate or severe pain (>50 on a 100 point visual analog scale) and a successful trial of spinal cord stimulation. However, a crossover randomized trial identified 50 adults with chonic severe pain following lumbar spine surgery and implanted a pulsd generator. They found no difference between real and sham stimulation periods, with both groups improving by 10 points on a 100 point scale.
There is no evidence to support the efficacy of local anesthetic sympathetic blockade for complex regional pain syndrome.

A systematic review looked at the evidence for surgical treatment of 14 chronic painful musculoskeletal conditions (i.e., spinal stenosis, and hip, knee, back, shoulder and wrist pain). Studies comparing surgery with no treatment of sham procedure generally found no benefit for chronic shoulder pain, pain from carpal tunnel syndrome, knee meniscectomy or debridement, or surgery for back pain. Knee replacement was effective.

ACP guidelines recommend the following for patients with chronic low back pain before considering medical therapy: yoga, tai chi, mindfulness, exercise, acupuncture, progress relaxation, biofeedback, low-level laser therapy, and spinal mannipulation, all based on low-level evidence.

A randomized trial of mindfulness therapy in 811 US veterans with chronic pain (delivered via pre-recorded, weekly videos) found that it is effective to decrease loss of function in patients with chronic pain. Delivering the videos in groups was no more effective than having individuals watch the videos on their own, though both methods involved having trained facilitators reach out to participants; that is, they were not just given a website and told to get started.

Mind-Body treatments: A systematic review found that mind-body treatments such as meditation, hypnosis, therapeutic suggestion and cognitive behavioral therapy reduce pain scores in patients taking opioids and may decrease the duration or amount of opioid needed.

Acupuncture: An RCT of acupuncture found it no better than sham acupuncture in relieving pain of fibromyalgia. A systematic review of patients with chronic knee pain similarly found no benefit to laser or needle acupuncture. However, a meta-analysis of four RCTs for chronic painful conditions found a moderate benefit of acupuncture ompared with no acupuncture control (effect size 0.5 SD). The effect was smaller (0.2 SD) but still significant when the comparison group received sham acupuncture.
Lasers: Low-level laser therapy improves neck pain.
Music: There is low quality evidence that music therapy reduces pain and anxiety post-operatively.
Spinal manipulation therapy: A review of 39 randomized controlled trials found no evidence that spinal manipulation therapy is superior to other standard treatments for chronic low back pain.

Vitamin D: A Cochrane review of vitamin D found no evidence of benefit from 10 studies with 811 participants. An RCT of 251 adults with chronic pain similarly found no benefit to vitamin D supplementation.
Non-drug treatments, such as physical therapy, are useful for musculoskeletal pain, even as drug therapy is being initiated.
An RCT comparing acupuncture with therapeutic massage and education for patients with chronic back pain found that only massage was effective.

Exercise has been shown to improve symptoms in fibromyalgia, with strength building more effective than flexibility training. The advice to continue activity as tolerated is effective in maintaining functionality in patients with chronic back pain.
A systematic review of six RCTs concluded that elastic taping was not effective for chronic pain due to knee osteoarthritis.
A systematic review concluded that multimodal physical therapy lowered pain intensity in women with chronic pelvic pain.

Psychological therapies, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), have shown some benefits in chronic headaches in adolescents and children, in fibromyalgia patients, and in veterans with chronic pain disorders.

A systematic review identified 54 RCTs with 5463 patients comparing in-person with remotely delivered CBT and found little or no difference in effectiveness (standardized mean difference -0.02, 95%CI -0.12 to 0.07).

Mindfulness and self-hypnosis have been shown to be helpful in acute pain, and are being used for chronic pain management. A Cochrane review of mind and body therapy (e.g., biofeedback, mindfulness, relaxation) for fibromyalgia found some evidence of benefit but overall low quality evidence.

A trial randomized 230 military personnel to mindfulness based therapy or supportive psychotherapy. Those receiving MBT had a larger daily opioid dose reduction (21% vs 4%), and also reduced anhedonia, catastrophizing behaviors, and cravings more than supportive psychotherapy.

Another study in US veterans randomized 811 to mindfulness-based intervention, in group or self-paced sessions, delivered via videoconference or to receive usual care. The interventions were effective at reducing loss of function.
A Cochrane systematic review found that behavioral therapies are minimally effective, but that cognitive behavioral therapy has small to moderate effects on pain, mood, and disability.

When added to methadone treatment, a mindfulness intervention delivered via telehealth improved outcomes including drug use, pain, depression, treatment retention, and adherence compared with methadone alone.
Treatment should not only emphasize management of painful symptoms, but also maintaining functionality and continued participation in society.
The first goal of pain treatment is to correct any underlying cause of the pain. In patients with chronic pain, this step has generally already been taken.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). A review of 19 RCTs was inconclusive. There is limited and inconsistent evidence to support its use for chronic low back pain.
Spinal cord stimulation may be effective for patients with complex regional pain syndrome and who have failed back surgery.
Common adverse effects of chronic opioids use include dry mouth (25%), nausea (21%), and constipation (15%). Approximately one in five patients withdrew from studies due to adverse events.

Consequences of poorly managed pain include reduced quality of life and productivity, depression, social isolation, sleep disturbance, decreased ambulation, and increased health care utilization and cost.
With appropriate treatment, many chronic pain patients can maintain function, and continue to participate in activities of daily living. Many patients remain employed.
Patients on long-term opioids require careful monitoring. A drug contract that outlines your expectations and gives their informed consent for use of a controlled substance should be used.
The elderly suffer chronic pain more frequently than other populations, but it may be under-reported and under-treated. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients over 65.

Acetaminophen is considered the safest pain medication in pregnancy. Ibuprofen is pregnancy category B, but is to be avoided in the first trimester and the second half of the third trimester. The other NSAIDs are pregnancy category C.
Oxycodone is pregnancy category B. The other opioids are pregnancy category C, but are used when there is not a better alternative.

A Cochrane review identified 29 RCTs of psychological therapies for pain in children. They are effective and the benefits are long-lasting. Therapies studied included hypnosis, coping skills training, biofeedback, and cognitive behavioral therapy.
